stops.name: Marriage to Teresa Caterina Destito
stops.campa: In the same year as his chair, Vico marries Teresa Caterina Destito, a childhood friend of the neighborhood, unlettered but, he will say, of a strength and good sense that carried the household through poverty he could never fully lift with a rhetorician's stipend. Eight children follow across the years, not all of whom survive childhood, and hardship visits the household more than once before the end. Of the household's daily arithmetic, pawned rings and unpaid rents against the price of paper and print, Vico says almost nothing directly in his own account; the New Science, when it comes, will be paid for out of exactly this scarcity.

stops.name: The annual orations: teaching the young of Naples
stops.campa: Each October, opening the academic year, the professor of eloquence delivers before the assembled students of the Studi a formal oration on the aims of study and the good life of the mind: six of these survive from his first years in the chair, urging the young toward a wisdom that joins eloquence to virtue and knowledge to civic use, against the narrow specialist who knows much and understands little. Vico is, by his own account, a poor and hesitant public speaker, plain rather than polished, and yet these annual addresses to the students of Naples become, oration by oration, the workshop in which his whole philosophy of education and history is first hammered into shape.

stops.name: De nostri temporis studiorum ratione
stops.campa: On the eighteenth of October, marking the university's formal reopening, Vico delivers his seventh and most consequential inaugural oration, On the Study Methods of Our Time. Against the reigning Cartesian fashion, which prizes the geometrical method and the critical faculty above all, he argues for the older art of topics, the training of memory, imagination, and a quick sense of the probable and the concrete, without which no student ever learns prudence, eloquence, or the capacity to judge particular human affairs. The mathematical method that sharpens judgment about lines and numbers, he warns his audience, can atrophy the very faculties that govern courts, cities, and nations.

stops.name: De antiquissima Italorum sapientia: verum ipsum factum
stops.campa: Working alone in Naples on the etymologies of the old Italic tongues, Vico publishes the first part of a metaphysics he means to found on the wisdom buried in the Latin language itself, and states there, in four Latin words, the axiom the whole New Science will be built upon: the true and the made are convertible. Only the maker of a thing can fully know it; God alone truly knows nature, which He made, while men can truly know only what men themselves have made, which is history, language, law, and the civil world of nations. The axiom sounds abstract; it will turn out to be the key to everything that follows.

stops.name: De uno universi juris principio et fine uno
stops.campa: Still hoping to be called at last to the chair of civil law, Vico publishes the first volume of a projected universal jurisprudence, arguing that all positive law, however various among the nations, descends from one single principle and aims at one single end: the justice that providence works into human affairs across time, whether men know it or not. It is a lawyer's treatise built like a metaphysics and a metaphysics built like a history of law; readers accustomed to ordinary legal commentary do not know quite what shelf to put it on, and the book that was meant to win him a chair wins him instead a narrower and stranger readership.

stops.name: De constantia iurisprudentis
stops.campa: A second volume follows, De constantia iurisprudentis, in which Vico turns from the single principle of law to the constancy of the jurist's own judgment across the changes of nations: how a Roman praetor, a feudal baron's magistrate, and a modern Neapolitan judge can all be said to practice one continuous art of equity, though the customs, weapons, and languages around them are unrecognizable from one age to the next. The three ages he will later name gods, heroes, and men are already visible here, half-formed, moving beneath the technical apparatus of a lawbook few outside Naples will ever read.

stops.name: The Notae, the third volume closes the work
stops.campa: Vico closes Il Diritto Universale with a volume of Notae, annotations and clarifications answering objections and tightening the argument of the two books before it, a scholar's habit of returning to correct and complete rather than simply moving on to the next title. He is fifty-four, three heavy Latin volumes deep into a case for the chair he covets, and still without it. The books have cost him money he cannot easily spare and bought him a small circle of admirers in the Republic of Letters, but not, so far, the one appointment that would let him teach what he actually believes.

stops.name: The competition for the chair of civil law, lost
stops.campa: The morning chair of civil law falls vacant at last and Vico competes for it before the assembled Studi, certain that three published volumes of jurisprudence must weigh more than rivals with better family connections and no comparable body of work. He has no patron in the vice-regal government; the post goes to Domenico Gentile. It is the bitterest disappointment of his professional life, and, by his own later account, the hinge of his second and greater turn: robbed of the career he wanted, he sits down instead to gather everything he has read and thought, at Vatolla and after, into a single new science of nations.

stops.name: The ring sold, the first Scienza Nuova printed
stops.campa: Unable to find a patron willing to underwrite the printing, Vico sells his one gold ring to pay the press, and the Principj di una Scienza Nuova intorno alla natura delle nazioni appears in Naples in a modest, badly funded edition: the discovery, he announces, of a new science of the common nature of nations, built on the axiom that men can truly know only the civil world they themselves have made. He sends copies out to scholars across Italy and beyond, hoping for the recognition Naples has withheld; most of the learned world does not yet know what to do with it.

stops.name: Poetic wisdom: the first men, children of the world
stops.campa: At the heart of the new science stands its strangest and most fertile claim: the first men of the gentile nations, unable yet to reason abstractly, thought in bodies and passions, imagining thunder as an angry god and the sky itself as a great animated body watching them; this poetic wisdom, sapienza poetica, is not primitive error to be outgrown but the very faculty, the imaginative universal, out of which law, religion, and language are first made. The nations do not begin with philosophers. They begin, every one of them, as poets who do not yet know they are speaking in metaphor.

stops.name: The three ages: gods, heroes, and men
stops.campa: Out of the study of Rome, of the Greeks, of the barbarian kingdoms after the fall of empire, and of his own Naples, Vico draws the pattern he believes governs every nation without exception: an age of gods, in which oracles and rites rule savage families through fear of the divine; an age of heroes, in which a warrior nobility holds law and land against the common people by force dressed as custom; and an age of men, in which reason, equality, and written law finally prevail, until the nation, grown too rational and too soft, falls back toward a new barbarism and the cycle turns again.

stops.name: The Second New Science and the dipintura
stops.campa: Vico rewrites the whole work almost from the ground up for a second edition, clearer in argument and richer in the philology of Homer, Roman law, and the feudal chronicles, and opens it with an emblematic frontispiece, the dipintura, designed with his Neapolitan friend the sculptor Domenico Antonio Vaccaro: a ray from the eye of divine providence striking the breast of metaphysics, a broken statue of Homer, the instruments of the nations' arts arranged around a globe. He spends eighty pages explaining, image by image, what the engraving means, insisting that the whole science can be read, compressed, in that single sheet before a single sentence of prose.
